text.p: Austria's Creditanstalt, taking stock of its last year as an independent bank, on Wednesday reported a 35 percent rise in 1996 net profit and said its new owner and former foe Bank Austria could expect more good news this year.

The one-time banker to the Austro-Hungarian empire fell prey to its closest competitor in January when the Austrian government sold its 69.45 percent voting stake in Creditanstalt to market leader Bank Austria for 17.2 billion schillings ($1.4 billion) in cash.

The bank said its strong international operations helped to boost 1996 group net profit to a record 2.93 billion schillings from 2.166 billion a year earlier. Group operating profit rose to 6.468 billion from 6.138 billion in 1995.

Creditanstalt said the positive trend continued in the first quarter of this year when operating profit, boosted by strong trading results, jumped to 2.2 billion schillings from 1.61 billion in the first three months of 1995.

"In 1997, profit after taxes is likely to rise for the fifth year in succession," Creditanstalt said. It traced most of the increase to cost-cutting and lower risk provisions, which in 1996 alone dipped to 3.1 billion schillings from 3.4 billion the year before.
But in spite of the sparkling figures, outgoing chief executive Guido Schmidt-Chiari sounded a melancholic note.
"It's a good result. It gives us particular satisfaction because a completely new era has dawned in the 142-year long history of Creditanstalt," he told a news conference.

Schmidt-Chiari, who has indicated he will step down at the bank's extraordinary shareholders meeting on Friday, was among the most vociferous opponents of Creditanstalt's sale to Bank Austria which closed the book on Europe's longest-running privatisation drama.
"Creditanstalt was an attractive bride. Now we have been married off with a rather large dowry," he said.
Asked whether the bank was facing a bright future, he added: "I sure hope so, I would wish it for her. After all, we're still her lovers."

Schmidt-Chiari said one of his greatest achievements during his nine-year tenure at the bank's helm had been to steer its expansion in central and eastern Europe after the fall of the Iron Curtain in 1989.
In the past year, international business contributed around one third of group operating profit and more than one third of net profit.
Creditanstalt said it would pay a dividend of 12 schillings per share for 1996, up from 10 schillings a year earlier.
Schmidt-Chiari admitted the strong rise in earnings would have warranted a bigger dividend increase, but hinted that the 1996 dividend level had been dictated by Bank Austria.
"A higher payout would have been possible, but of course the new majority owner has a word to say in this," he said.

Investors appeared to take a neutral stance on the bank's results. In midday trade on the Vienna bourse, the Creditanstalt preference stock was up one schilling at 458, while its ordinaries were down four schillings at 719. ($ = 12.08 Austrian Schillings)
